entry: [[Polymer|Synthetic polymer]] of the aromatic hydrocarbon styrene, one of the most widely used [[Plastic|plastics]]. General-purpose polystyrene is clear, hard and brittle, and it can be solid or foamed. It is relatively cheap but a poor barrier to [[Oxygen|oxygen]] and [[Water|water]] vapor. It flows when heated above about 100 °C, its glass transition temperature, so it can be [[Extrusion|extruded]], molded or vacuum formed. Uses include packing peanuts, [[Optical disc|optical disc]] cases and disposable [[Cutlery|cutlery]]. It was discovered in 1839 by Eduard Simon. Under ASTM standards it is not biodegradable, and it accumulates as litter, especially in [[Foam|foam]] form, along shores, waterways and in the oceans.

Synthetic [[Polymer|polymer]] of tetrafluoroethylene, valued for its heat resistance and chemical inertness. Known by the brand name Teflon, it was invented by [[DuPont]], and Roy J. Plunkett discovered it accidentally in 1938 while working for the company. It is hydrophobic and has one of the lowest coefficients of [[Friction|friction]] of any [[Solid|solid]]. It is used as a non-stick coating for cookware, as a lining for containers and pipework that handle corrosive chemicals, and in expanded porous form as a surgical graft material. PTFE is among the best-known [[PFAS]]. DuPont later stopped using perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in production after legal action over its health and ecotoxicological effects.

Belief in or worship of more than one [[Deity|deity]]. It contrasts with [[Monotheism|monotheism]], belief in a single, usually transcendent deity. The term was coined by the Jewish writer Philo of Alexandria from the Greek roots for many and god. Polytheistic religions often have a pantheon of deities, which may represent natural forces or ancestral principles. Some polytheists focus worship on one deity while recognizing others, a position called monolatry, kathenotheism or henotheism. Polytheism was common in the time and place of the [[Abrahamic religions]], and the [[Quran]] explicitly denounces it. Notable polytheistic religions practiced today include [[Taoism]], Chinese folk religion, [[Shinto]] and neopagan faiths such as [[Wicca]]. [[Hinduism]] cannot be categorized exclusively as polytheistic, since some Hindus consider their beliefs monotheistic or pantheistic.

Class of [[Polymer|polymers]] made of organic units joined by carbamate (urethane) links. Polyurethanes are formed by reacting a diisocyanate with a polyol, and varied starting materials produce many different polymers within the group. Applications include rigid and flexible [[Foam|foams]], coatings, adhesives, electrical potting compounds and fibers such as spandex. Foams accounted for 67% of all polyurethane produced in 2016. Otto Bayer and his coworkers at IG Farben in Germany first made polyurethanes in 1937. Global production in 2019 was 25 million metric tonnes, about 6% of all polymers produced that year.

Synthetic [[Polymer|polymer]] that is the world's third-most widely produced plastic, after [[Polyethylene|polyethylene]] and polypropylene. About 40 million tons are produced each year. Rigid PVC is used for pipes, doors and windows, and plasticizers make it softer for [[Electrical cable|cable]] insulation, flooring, signage and inflatable products. About 80% of production uses suspension polymerization of vinyl chloride monomer. PVC is about 57% [[Chlorine|chlorine]] by mass, and it is a white, brittle solid. Waldo Semon and the B.F. Goodrich Company developed a method in 1926 to plasticize PVC by blending it with additives. It is also used in [[Plumbing|plumbing]] and, blended with cotton or linen, in [[Canvas|canvas]].

Fruit-bearing deciduous shrub or tree in the family Lythraceae, *Punica granatum*. It is rich in symbolic and mythological associations and is mentioned in the Old Testament. It originated in the region spanning the [[Caucasus]] and the [[Iranian plateau]], where ancient Iranians first domesticated it about 5,000 years ago. It grows 1.5 to 5 metres (4.9 to 16.4 ft) tall and is extensively cultivated for its fruit in much of Asia, Africa, the Mediterranean basin, the United States and Chile. Spanish settlers introduced it to California in 1769. The fruit is typically in season in the Northern Hemisphere from September to February. Pomegranate molasses is a key ingredient in Persian cuisine, and the fruit and its juice are used in [[Baking|baking]], juice blends and [[Cocktail|cocktails]].

Largest [[Citrus|citrus]] fruit, *Citrus maxima*, native to Southeast Asia. It is a natural, non-hybrid citrus and an ancestor of several cultivated species, including the [[Orange (fruit)|bitter orange]] and the [[Grapefruit|grapefruit]]. Typically 63% of the grapefruit's genome comes from the pomelo. The fruit is 10–30 centimetres (4–12 inches) in diameter, with a thicker peel and less acidic flesh than a grapefruit. It is commonly eaten and used for festive occasions throughout Southeast and East Asia. Like the grapefruit, it contains phytochemicals with potential for drug interactions.

Ancient city near modern [[Naples]], Italy, buried in the [[Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD|eruption of Mount Vesuvius]] in AD 79. It was buried under 4 to 6 m (13 to 20 ft) of volcanic ash and [[Pumice|pumice]], and before that it had been a wealthy town of 10,000 to 20,000 residents. Its preservation offers a snapshot of Roman life and of [[Urban planning|urban planning]]. Organic remains, including human bodies, decayed in the ash, leaving cavities that archaeologists used to create molds of figures in their final moments. Graffiti preserves examples of the colloquial Vulgar Latin spoken in the city. Oscans founded five villages on the site in the 8th century BC, and Greeks arrived in Campania from around 740 BC. Rediscovered in the late 16th century, it was excavated systematically only from the mid-18th century, the start of modern archaeology. Pompeii is a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] and attracts approximately 2.5 million visitors a year.

Roman general and statesman prominent in the final decades of the [[Roman Republic]]. A protégé of the dictator [[Sulla]], he won military success in the civil war of 83–81 BC, and Sulla granted him the cognomen Magnus, "the Great," reportedly reflecting his admiration for [[Alexander the Great]]. He was elected consul three times (70, 55 and 52 BC) and celebrated three triumphs. In 60 BC he joined [[Marcus Licinius Crassus|Crassus]] and [[Julius Caesar|Caesar]] in the First Triumvirate, cemented by his marriage to Caesar's daughter, Julia. After the deaths of Julia and Crassus in 54 and 53 BC, he allied himself with the optimates, a conservative faction of the Senate. His conflict with Caesar led to civil war, and Pompey was defeated at Pharsalus in 48 BC. He fled to Egypt, where he was assassinated by courtiers of Ptolemy XIII.

Small, still, land-based body of water formed by pooling in a depression, naturally or artificially. A pond is smaller than a [[Lake|lake]], and no official criteria distinguish the two. Some definitions treat a pond as less than 5 hectares (12 acres) in area, less than 5 metres (16 ft) deep and with under 30% of its area covered by emergent vegetation. Ponds form by processes such as cutoff river channels on [[Floodplain|floodplains]], glacial action, or [[Beaver|beaver]] activity. Typically shallow and freshwater, ponds support algae, snails, fish, [[Amphibian|amphibian]] larvae, frogs, turtles and otters. Ponds that dry up each year, killing resident fish, provide refugia for amphibian breeding and are often called vernal pools. Many ponds are made by people, for uses such as providing water for agriculture and livestock, habitat restoration and flood control. Ponds can also act as sources and sinks of [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]].

Capital and most populous city of the Union Territory of Puducherry, India, on the southeast coast. Its name derives from Tamil for "new village"; the French first spelled it Poudichéry. Founded as a French trading settlement in 1674 by François Martin, it served as the capital of French India. The city lies on the [[Bay of Bengal]] and is bordered by [[Tamil Nadu]], with which it shares most of its culture, heritage and language. Its territory was transferred de facto to India in 1954. Its colonial-era architecture and the nearby [[Sri Aurobindo]] Ashram draw visitors.

Free-floating aquatic plant, *Pontederia crassipes*, native to tropical [[South America]] and often [[Invasive species|invasive]] elsewhere. It has glossy leaves and buoyant, bulb-like stalks, and it may rise as much as 1 m (3 ft) above the water. One of the fastest-growing plants known, it spreads by runners and by seeds that can remain viable for more than 28 years, and its mats can double in size in one to two weeks. Introduced to many regions, it can cover ponds and lakes, blocking light and displacing native plants. Fresh plants contain [[Hydrogen cyanide|hydrogen cyanide]] and alkaloids, and frost kills the leaves. Control methods include mechanical harvesting, herbicides and biological agents such as Neochetina [[Weevil|weevils]], which have reduced its biomass in field trials.

Roman governor of Judaea under Emperor [[Tiberius]], from 26/27 to 36/37 AD. He presided over the trial of [[Jesus]] and ordered his [[Crucifixion of Jesus|crucifixion]], as the Gospels, [[Josephus]] and [[Tacitus]] attribute. Surviving evidence includes coins he minted and the Pilate Stone inscription. Josephus reports that he was dismissed after violently quelling a Samaritan uprising, and that Tiberius died before he could reach Rome. Historians differ on his rule, with some viewing him as brutal and inept and others citing his long tenure as evidence of moderate competence. Some Eastern traditions depict him as a Christian convert and saint, while Western texts often portrayed him negatively. He has appeared in art and modern literature, including works by [[Mikhail Bulgakov]].

Small [[Horse|horse]] usually under a specified height at full maturity. Ponies typically have thicker coats, manes and tails, and proportionally shorter legs, wider barrels and heavier bone than larger horses. For competition, the International Federation for Equestrian Sports sets the cutoff at 148 centimetres (58.3 in; 14.2 hands) without shoes. Many pony breeds developed in cold, harsh climates, and they are hardy, easy keepers that need only half the [[Hay|hay]] of a horse for their weight. Ponies are remarkably strong for their size, and properly trained ponies suit children learning to ride, while larger ponies can carry adults. They are more vulnerable to laminitis and Cushing's syndrome. The word derives from the old French poulenet, a diminutive of poulain, meaning foal.

Type of financial [[Fraud|fraud]], named after Italian con artist Charles Ponzi. It pays apparent profits to earlier [[Investment|investors]] from funds contributed by more recent ones. It misleads investors either by falsely claiming that profits come from legitimate business when the business activities are non-existent, or by exaggerating the profitability of real activities. The scheme can sustain the illusion of a viable business only while new funds keep arriving and most investors do not demand full repayment or lose faith in the assets.

Breed of water dog with a thick, curly coat that comes in many colors and patterns. Poodles are divided into Standard, Medium, Miniature and Toy varieties by size. They are active and intelligent and are especially able to learn from humans, and they tend to live 10–18 years. The breed probably originated in [[Germany]], though the Fédération Cynologique Internationale and some cynologists credit [[France]]. Larger poodles retrieved game from water for wildfowl hunters, and smaller ones were circus performers. Poodles were the American Kennel Club's most registered breed from 1960 to 1982.

Family of [[Cue sports|cue sports]] played on a billiard table with six pockets along the rails. Eight-ball is the most frequently played discipline and is often treated as synonymous with pool. Other popular games include nine-ball, ten-ball, straight pool, one-pocket and bank pool. The generic term pocket billiards is broader, covering games such as [[Snooker|snooker]], Russian pyramid and Kaisa, which are not called pool. Hybrid games combine pool and carom billiards, including English billiards.

Art movement of the mid-to-late 1950s in the [[United Kingdom]] and [[United States]]. It brought imagery from popular and mass culture, including [[Advertising|advertising]], [[Comics|comics]], product packaging and celebrities, into painting, sculpture and printmaking. By elevating the banal and mass-produced to high art, it blurred the boundary between high and low culture, often using mechanical means of reproduction. British artists such as Eduardo Paolozzi and Richard Hamilton worked in collage and painting, and by the early 1960s [[Andy Warhol]], Roy Lichtenstein and Tom Wesselmann had brought it international prominence. Pop art is widely seen as both a reaction against and an extension of [[Abstract expressionism|abstract expressionism]], and it drew on [[Dada]] precedents.

Variety of corn kernel that puffs up when heated, and the snack made from it. Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks, with evidence dating back thousands of years in the Americas. Its strong hull encloses starchy endosperm with 14–20% moisture, which turns to steam as the kernel heats until the hull ruptures and the kernel expands to 20 to 50 times its original size. Strains cultivated for popping are mainly *Zea mays* variety *everta*, a special kind of flint corn. Popcorn is commonly eaten [[Salt|salted]], [[Butter|buttered]], sweetened or with artificial flavorings.

Bishop of Rome and head of the worldwide [[Catholic Church]]. The office is called the papacy, and its jurisdiction is the [[Holy See]], a sovereign entity under international law. From the 8th century until 1870, popes were sovereigns of the [[Papal States]], and since 1929 they have headed the much smaller [[Vatican City]] state. Catholic tradition holds that [[Saint Peter]] and Saint Paul founded the see in the first century. Temporal influence declined over time, while claims of spiritual authority grew, culminating in the 1870 proclamation of papal infallibility for formal definitions of faith or morals. The pope is considered one of the world's most powerful people, with influence over 1.4 billion Catholics. Leo XIV was elected on 8 May 2025.

Head of the [[Catholic Church]] from 1492 to 1503 and sovereign of the [[Papal States]]. Born Roderic de Borja in the Kingdom of Valencia, he was a member of the Borgia family and studied law at the University of Bologna. Papal bulls of 1493 confirmed the rights of the Spanish crown in the New World after the discoveries of [[Christopher Columbus]]. During the second Italian war he supported his son [[Cesare Borgia]] as a condottiero for the French king. Alexander is one of the most controversial Renaissance popes, partly because he acknowledged several children by his mistresses, and his surname Borgia became a byword for libertinism and nepotism.

Head of the [[Catholic Church]] and sovereign of Vatican City from 2005 until his resignation in 2013. Born Joseph Alois Ratzinger, he became a leading theologian and was made prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in 1981. As pope he advocated a return to fundamental Christian values, calling relativism's denial of objective truth the central problem of the 21st century. He permitted greater use of the Tridentine Mass, promoted [[Latin]] and reintroduced traditional papal vestments. He was the first pope to resign since Gregory XII in 1415. Critics, including public health officials, objected to his handling of sexual abuse cases and his opposition to condoms.

Head of the [[Catholic Church]] and leader of the Papal States from 1294 to 1303. Born into the Caetani family, he succeeded Pope Celestine V, who had abdicated, and he put forward some of the strongest papal claims to temporal as well as spiritual power. He quarreled with [[Philip IV of France]] and with Albert I of Germany, and he excommunicated Philip. In 1303 Philip's troops seized him at Anagni, and he died a month later. Boniface systematized canon law in the *Liber Sextus* (1298) and established the first Catholic jubilee year in Rome. [[Dante Alighieri|Dante]] expected him to arrive among the simoniacs in the eighth circle of Hell in the *Divine Comedy*.

Head of the [[Catholic Church]] from 2013 to 2025. The first Jesuit pope and the first from Latin America, he was born and raised in Buenos Aires and chose the name Francis in honor of [[Francis of Assisi]]. He was noted for humility, concern for the poor, migrants and refugees, and interreligious dialogue. He made action on [[Climate change|climate change]] a leading focus, viewed capital punishment as inadmissible in all cases, and committed the church to its worldwide abolition. He permitted non-liturgical blessings of individuals in same-sex relationships. He helped restore diplomatic relations between Cuba and the United States, and he signed the Vatican's first treaty with Palestine.

64th bishop of Rome, from 590 to 604, known as Saint Gregory the Great. A Roman senator's son, he was prefect of Rome at 30 before becoming a papal ambassador and then pope. His administration greatly improved the welfare of Rome's people. He regained papal authority in Spain and France, and he sent missionaries to England, including Augustine of Canterbury. Franks, [[Lombards|Lombards]] and [[Visigoths|Visigoths]] aligned with Rome in religion, a realignment that shaped medieval Europe. He combated the [[Heresy|Donatist heresy]] and revised the Roman liturgy, so that he was known in the Middle Ages as the Father of Christian Worship. Along with Augustine, [[Jerome]] and [[Ambrose]], he is one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers.
